Outline

Discounted Dividend Valuation ​

Choosing which cash flow to discount (dividends, free cash flow or residual income); the Gordon growth model, PVGO and justified P/E; multistage dividend discount models (two-stage, H-model, three-stage, spreadsheet); implied growth and implied required return; and sustainable growth.

Choosing the Cash Flow ​

Cash flowMost suitable whenProblems
DividendsThe company pays dividends; the board's policy has a clear, consistent link to profitability; a non-control (minority) perspectiveNon-payers; dividends unrelated to earnings
FCFE / FCFFNo dividends, or dividends far from FCFE; FCF tracks profitability within a comfortable forecast horizon; a control perspective (also when a takeover is possible)Heavy capex → FCF negative for many years
Residual incomeNo dividends, and FCF negative within the comfortable horizonNeeds detailed accrual accounting; distorted by poor accounting quality
FCFF=CFO−CapexEquity=PV(FCFF)−DebtFCFE=FCFF−Net payments to debtRIt=Et−r×Bt−1V0=B0+PV(RIt)Bt=Bt−1+Et−Dt
  • FCFF is the cash flow before debt (capex includes working capital). It is easier when leverage is expected to change a lot.
  • FCFE is the cash flow after debt; net payments are interest and principal, net of new debt.
  • Residual income usually recognizes value earlier than FCF models, and relies on the clean surplus relation.

Dividend Discount Model ​

For one period, n periods and forever:

V0=D1+P11+rV0=∑t=1nDt(1+r)t+Pn(1+r)nV0=∑t=1∞Dt(1+r)t

Dividends are assumed to be paid once, at the end of each period. Even an investor with a finite horizon depends on all future dividends, through the sale price Pn.

Example: Carrefour (One Period) ​

Carrefour is expected to pay a dividend of €0.46 next year and then trade at €23.00. The required return is 8%.

V0=D1+P11+r=0.46+23.001.08=21.72

V0 = €21.72.

Example: Five-Year Horizon ​

The required return is 10%, and the share is expected to sell for $40 at the end of Year 5.

Year12345
Dividend ($)2.002.102.203.503.75
PV at 10% ($)1.8181.7361.6532.3912.328
PV of dividends=1.818+1.736+1.653+2.391+2.328=9.926PV of price=401.105=24.837V0=9.926+24.837=34.76

V0 = $34.76.

There are two ways to make the infinite sum workable: (1) assume a stylized growth pattern (constant, two-stage, H-model, three-stage); or (2) forecast individual dividends for 3–10 years (depending on how visible earnings are), then add a terminal value from a growth model or a multiple.

Gordon Growth Model ​

V0=D0(1+g)r−g=D1r−g(r>g)

It assumes dividends grow at a constant rate g forever, with long-term r and g, and r>g. Value, dividends and (with a constant payout) earnings all grow at g, so g is also the capital gains yield, and the dividend yield stays constant.

IMPORTANT

Use D1, not D0, in the numerator. Use the GGM only when long-run g is at most nominal GDP growth (real growth + expected inflation); if expected growth is well above that, use a multistage model.

Example: Sonoco ​

Sonoco pays a quarterly dividend of $0.41, expected to grow at 4.5% a year. The risk-free rate is 3%, beta 0.95 and the equity risk premium 4.5%. The share trades at $59.55.

Step 1. Inputs.

D0=4×0.41=$1.64r=3%+0.95×4.5%=7.3%

Step 2. Value.

V0=1.64×1.0450.073−0.045=1.71380.028=$61.21

V0 = $61.21 is above the $59.55 price, so Sonoco is slightly undervalued.

Example: Middlesex Water (GGM) ​

Middlesex Water's dividend is D0 = $0.911, expected to grow at g = 4.5%; the price is $43.20. Every estimate of r below uses the same next dividend:

D1=0.911×1.045=$0.952
Estimate of rV0=D1/(r−g)Verdict
Analyst: 6.8%$41.39Within 5% → fairly valued
CAPM, adjusted β 0.80: 3% + 0.8(4.5%) = 6.6%$45.33Fairly valued (about 5% above)
Bond yield + premium: 4.8% + 2.5% = 7.3%$34.00Overvalued (but the premium is arbitrary)

The GGM fits Middlesex: a stable ROE (a regulated water utility), a consistent 60–70% payout, growth of 4.5% close to US nominal GDP growth (about 4.3%), and no period of abnormal growth. Its beta has an R2 below 20%, so the CAPM r is uncertain.

Sensitivity. Moving r and g by ±25 bp gives values from $33.92 to $53.02; value explodes as r−g shrinks.

g = 4.25%g = 4.50%g = 4.75%
r = 6.55%41.2946.4453.02
r = 6.80%37.2441.3946.55
r = 7.05%33.9237.3341.49

Other uses of the formula.

  • Perpetual preferred stock (non-callable, fixed rate): V0=D/r. A 4% preferred with $25 par pays $1.00 a year; at r = 5.5%:
V0=1.000.055=$18.18
  • Negative growth works too. Afton Mines: D1 = $4.25, g = −4%, r = 9%:
V0=4.250.09−(−0.04)=4.250.13=$32.69
StrengthsLimitations
Simple, easy to communicateVery sensitive to r and g
Fits mature, stable dividend payers and broad developed-market indexesUnusable for non-payers or unpredictable dividends
Gives the terminal value in multistage modelsInvalid if g≥r; unrealistic for high-growth companies
Can back out implied g or r

Implied Growth and Share Repurchases ​

  • Buybacks reduce the share count, but companies don't commit to buyback levels and time them opportunistically, so they're harder to forecast than dividends. At market prices, buybacks are neutral for remaining shareholders. A DDM still works if per-share dividend growth reflects the buybacks.
  • The implied growth rate solves P0=D0(1+g)/(r−g) for g:
g=rP0−D0P0+D0

Example: Implied Growth ​

A share trades at $40. Its beta is 1.1, the risk-free rate 5.6% and the equity risk premium 6%. The last dividend was $2.00, and the analyst expects 5% growth.

Step 1. Value at the analyst's growth rate.

r=5.6%+1.1×6%=12.2%V0=2.00×1.050.122−0.05=2.100.072=$29.17

Step 2. Growth implied by the price.

g=rP0−D0P0+D0=0.122×40−2.0040+2.00=2.8842=6.86%

The value ($29.17) is below the price ($40): the market prices in 6.86% growth, more than the analyst's 5%.

PVGO and Justified P/E ​

A share's value is the value of its assets in place, plus the present value of its growth opportunities:

V0=E1r+PVGOP0E1=1r+PVGOE1
  • E1/r is the no-growth value. A no-growth company has no positive-NPV projects, should pay out all its earnings, and its earnings stay flat.
  • Growth adds value only if new investment earns more than r (ROE > r). Reinvesting below r raises EPS but destroys value.
  • PVGO comes from investment opportunities and real options (timing, scale, abandonment).
  • A negative PVGO (e.g., Macy's, −$36.69 in early 2019) means the market expects value-destroying reinvestment, or that E1 is too high or r too low. By contrast, Alphabet's PVGO was 53% of its price and McDonald's 20%.

Example: Middlesex Water (PVGO) ​

Middlesex Water trades at $43.20, with forecast EPS E1 = $1.52 and r = 6.8%.

Step 1. Split the price.

E1r=1.520.068=$22.42PVGO=43.20−22.42=$20.78

Growth opportunities are 48% of the price.

Step 2. Split the P/E.

P0E1=43.201.52=28.4=10.068⏟14.7 no growth+20.781.52⏟13.67 growth

Justified P/E from the GGM, where b is the retention ratio and 1−b the payout:

Leading: P0E1=1−br−gTrailing: P0E0=(1−b)(1+g)r−g

For multistage models, the justified leading P/E is the model value ÷ E1.

Example: L'Oréal ​

InputValue
Price€242.70
E0 / D0€7.08 / €3.85
Payout 1−b3.85/7.08 = 0.5438
g4.25%
r2% + 0.72 × 5% = 5.6%

Step 1. Justified P/Es.

P0E1=0.54380.056−0.0425=40.28P0E0=0.5438×1.04250.0135=42.00

Step 2. Compare with the market.

Actual trailing P/E=242.707.08=34.3<42.0

L'Oréal is undervalued: equivalently, the GGM value 3.85×1.0425/0.0135 = €297.31 is above the €242.70 price.

Multistage Dividend Discount Models ​

PhaseGrowth and marginsFCFEPayout
GrowthRapidly expanding markets, high margins, very high EPS growthOften negative (heavy investment)Low or zero
TransitionGrowth slows toward the economy's (competition, saturation)Turns positive as capex fallsRising (or dividends begin)
MatureROE → r; stable growth, payout and ROEPositiveStable: the GGM applies

Two-Stage Model ​

V0=∑t=1nD0(1+gS)t(1+r)t+Vn(1+r)nVn=Dn+1r−gL=D0(1+gS)n(1+gL)r−gL

Steps: (1) list D1,…,Dn; (2) Dn+1=Dn(1+gL); (3) Vn=Dn+1/(r−gL); (4) discount everything at r. It fits a temporary advantage (a patent, first-mover status); its weakness is the abrupt drop in growth.

Example: Carl Zeiss Meditec ​

InputValue
D0€0.55
gS (Years 1–10) / gL (after)9% / 5%
r1.2% + 0.9 × 5.2% = 5.88%
Price€80.55

Step 1. Terminal value at Year 10.

D10=0.55×1.0910=1.302D11=1.302×1.05=1.3671V10=1.36710.0588−0.05=155.36

Step 2. Discount to today.

PV(V10)=155.361.058810=87.74PV of D1…D10=6.47V0=6.47+87.74=94.21

V0 = €94.21, above the €80.55 price; about 93% of it comes from the terminal value.

Terminal value can come from (1) the GGM on Dn+1, or (2) a multiple × a forecast fundamental (P/E × EPS, P/B × BVPS).

Example: P&G with a P/E Terminal Value ​

P&G's last dividend was $2.79, expected to grow 4% a year for 4 years; r = 6.5%. At Year 4 the payout ratio is expected to be 60% and the trailing P/E 22. The price is $96.47.

Step 1. Terminal value from the P/E.

D4=2.79×1.044=$3.2639EPS4=3.26390.60=$5.4398V4=22×5.4398=$119.68

Step 2. Discount to today.

PV(V4)=119.681.0654=$93.03PV of D1…D4=$10.52V0=10.52+93.03=$103.55

V0 = $103.55, above the $96.47 price.

Example: A Company That Doesn't Pay Yet ​

The first dividend, $1.00, is expected at t = 5, growing 5% a year after that; r = 11%.

V4=D5r−g=1.000.11−0.05=$16.67V0=16.671.114=$10.98

V0 = $10.98.

IMPORTANT

Vn=Dn+1/(r−g). If the first dividend is at t = 5, the GGM gives the value at t = 4, so discount 4 years, not 5.

H-Model ​

Growth starts at gS and declines linearly to gL over 2H years:

V0=D0(1+gL)r−gL+D0H(gS−gL)r−gL
  • The first term is the value if growth were gL from now; the second is the extra value from above-normal growth. It is an approximation, less accurate for a large H or a large gS−gL.
  • H is half the length of the high-growth period (10 years → H = 5).

Example: H-Model Value vs Price ​

A share trades at €41.70. D0 = €1.77; growth is 7%, declining linearly to 4% over 10 years (H = 5); r = 8%.

V0=1.77×1.040.08−0.04⏟normal growth+1.77×5×0.030.08−0.04⏟above-normal growth=1.840.04+0.270.04=46.00+6.75=52.75

V0 = €52.75, 26% above the price, so the share is undervalued.

Three-Stage Model ​

Version 1: three constant-growth stages. Grow D0 at g1, then g2, list each dividend, and cap the last stage with the GGM:

V0=∑t=1nDt(1+r)t+Dn(1+gL)/(r−gL)(1+r)n

Example: Three Constant-Growth Stages ​

D0 = $3.30 and r = 9%. Dividends grow 14% for 2 years, then 12% for 5 years, then 6.75% forever. The price is $194.98.

Step 1. Dividends through Year 7.

t1234567
g14%14%12%12%12%12%12%
Dt3.76204.28874.80335.37976.02536.74837.5581

Step 2. Terminal value at Year 7.

V7=7.5581×1.06750.09−0.0675=358.59PV(V7)=358.591.097=196.16

Step 3. Add.

V0=26.66⏟PV(D1…D7)+196.16=$222.82

V0 = $222.82, more than 14% above the price; the terminal value is about 88% of the value.

Version 2: a constant first stage, then an H-model for stages 2 and 3. Steps: (1) PV of the stage-1 dividends; (2) the H-model value at the start of stage 2, using Dn; (3) discount that to t = 0; (4) add.

Vn=Dn(1+gL)+DnH(gS−gL)r−gLV0=∑t=1nDt(1+r)t+Vn(1+r)n

Example: Rhinestone Energy ​

InputValue
Price$56.18
D0$0.56
Stage 111% for 5 years
Stages 2–3Declining linearly to 6.5% over 10 years (H = 5)
r3% + 1.2 × 4.2% = 8%
Fair-value band±20% of value

Step 1. Dividend at the end of stage 1.

D5=0.56×1.115=$0.9436

Step 2. H-model value at Year 5.

V5=0.9436×1.0650.08−0.065+0.9436×5×0.0450.08−0.065=66.9979+14.1545=$81.1524PV(V5)=81.15241.085=$55.2310

Step 3. Add the stage-1 dividends.

V0=3.0422⏟PV(D1…D5)+55.2310=$58.27

Stage 1 is 5.2% of the value; stages 2–3 are 94.8%.

Step 4. Compare. The band $58.27 × (0.8 to 1.2) = $46.62–$69.92 contains the $56.18 price, so Rhinestone is fairly valued.

What if the Year-2 dividend stays flat? Then D5 = $0.8501, V5 = $73.1103 and V0 = $52.56.

Bloomberg uses version 2 with growth plus transition fixed at 17 years: explosive 3/14, high 5/12, average 7/10, slow/mature 9/8.

Choosing a Model ​

ModelUse when
GGMMature; growth at or below nominal GDP; stable payout
Two-stageHigh growth for a set period, then an abrupt fall (e.g., patent expiry)
H-modelHigh growth declining gradually to maturity
Three-stageDistinct growth, transition and mature phases (younger companies)
SpreadsheetAny irregular pattern (asset sales, special dividends, detailed forecasts)

Example: Yang Co. (Irregular Dividends) ​

r = 12%. Dividends fall 10% a year after Year 1, jump in Year 5 on an asset sale, then grow 5% a year after Year 7.

Year1234567
Dividend ($)21.0018.9017.0115.3160.0040.0040.00

Step 1. Terminal value at Year 7.

V7=40×1.050.12−0.05=$600PV(V7)=6001.127=$271.41

Step 2. Add the PV of the seven dividends ($128.06).

V0=128.06+271.41=$399.48

Limitations of multistage models: the terminal value is often over 75% of the value and very sensitive to r and g, and the life-cycle picture is crude when technology changes fast.

Spreadsheet Modeling ​

Forecast sales, margins, interest, tax, payout and the balance sheet → dividends → discount them, with a terminal value from a multiple.

Example: Hoshino Distributors ​

Hoshino has sales of $100m and 4m shares; r = 15%, and the terminal P/E is 10.

AssumptionY1Y2Y3Y4Y5
Sales growth20%15%10%10%
EBIT margin20%20%18%16%16%
Payout20%20%30%40%50%

Interest is 10% of debt, tax 40%, and total assets 80% of sales.

Step 1. Forecast net income and dividends.

Y1Y2Y3Y4Y5
Net income ($m)9.6011.5011.6911.1912.32
DPS ($)0.4800.5750.8771.1201.540
PV at 15% ($)0.4170.4350.5770.6400.766

Step 2. Terminal value from the P/E.

EPS5=12.324=$3.08P5=10×3.08=$30.80PV(P5)=30.801.155=$15.31

Step 3. Add.

V0=2.84⏟PV of DPS+15.31=$18.15

Required Return from a DDM ​

Given the price, the required return is the IRR the model implies. For the GGM and the H-model:

r=D1P0+gr=D0P0[(1+gL)+H(gS−gL)]+gL

Examples: Implied Required Return ​

CaseInputsRequired return
NextEra (GGM)D0 $5.00, g 5.5%, P0 $169.835.00×1.055169.83+5.5%=3.11%+5.50%= 8.60%
GGMD1 $0.50, g 8%, P0 $100.5010+8%= 13%
H-modelD0 $1, P0 $20, 10% declining to 6% over 10 years (H = 5)120[1.06+5×0.04]+6%= 12.3%

For other multistage models, find r by trial and error (or Goal Seek) so that the PV equals the price.

Example: J&J (Trial and Error) ​

J&J's last dividend was $3.60, growing 7% for 6 years and then 5%; the price is $136.61.

Step 1. First guess from the GGM.

r≈3.60×1.07136.61+5%=7.8%

This must be too low: early growth is above 5%, so the true IRR is higher.

Step 2. Bracket the price.

rTwo-stage valuevs $136.61
8.0%$140.07Above: r too low
8.5%$119.92Below: r too high

Step 3. Interpolate. The IRR is just above 8%: r ≈ 8.08%.

NOTE

The IRR is the market-implied expected return; feeding it back into the DDM as r is circular. If the price differs from value, the expected return also includes the price converging to value.

Sustainable Growth ​

g=b×ROE

The sustainable growth rate is the growth that retained earnings alone can fund, with a constant capital structure and no new equity. Strictly, use the return on new investment and beginning equity. The PRAT model splits ROE with DuPont:

g=NI−DNI⏟R×NISales⏟P×SalesTA⏟A×TAEquity⏟T

Profit margin × asset turnover (P × A) = ROA, from operations; retention and leverage (R, T) reflect financial policy.

Example: Growth from Retention ​

ROE is 25%, the retention ratio 60%, and beginning equity $1,000,000.

g=0.60×25%=15%
This yearNext yearGrowth
Beginning equity1,000,0001,150,00015%
Net income (25%)250,000287,50015%
Dividends (40%)100,000115,00015%

Example: Baggai vs Mondale (PRAT) ​

Both companies have ROA (= P × A) of 10%.

Retention RROALeverage Tg=R×ROA×T
Baggai0.3010%1.253.75%
Mondale2/310%2.0013.33%

Mondale grows faster only because of its financial policy: more retention and more leverage.

Example: Mature-Phase Growth ​

Mature company. The payout is 25%, and ROE = r = 9%:

g=(1−0.25)×9%=6.75%

IBM. Its 2018 ROE of 52% was driven by leverage of 7.35, which won't last. Rebuild ROE from benchmark components, then apply a 50% payout:

ROE=10.5%⏟P×0.62⏟A×2.0⏟T=13.0%g=0.50×13.0%=6.5%

To estimate a mature-phase ROE: a DuPont forecast, ROE = r (no excess returns at maturity), or the median industry ROE.

Exam traps ​

  • g=b× ROE uses the retention ratio, not the payout.
  • An abnormally high historical ROE (often driven by leverage) won't last: forecast mature components.
  • Raising dividends faster than the sustainable growth rate needs external financing.

NOTE

Textbook typo. The L'Oréal solution prints the GGM value as 3.85(1.0425)/(0.05 − 0.0425); the result €297.31 only works with r = 0.056 (4.0136/0.0135 = 297.3).
